messages.content:
Title: Diagnosis
Details: The failure “CPIO reports unexpected EOF” during unarchiving is caused by how CpioArchiveInputStream handles end-of-entry padding and EOF conditions when reading entries.

Evidence and step-by-step:

1) Test behavior
- The failing test creates a CPIO with two files and then unpacks it by iterating:
  - getNextEntry()
  - IOUtils.copy(in, out) to copy the current entry’s payload until end-of-entry (signaled by read returning -1)
  - then repeats for the next entry.

2) How the reader determines end-of-entry and padding
- CpioArchiveInputStream.read(byte[], int, int) considers the entry finished when entryBytesRead == entry.getSize() (lines 253–266). At that point it:
  - Applies alignment padding (for “new” format, pad to 4 bytes; for “old binary”, pad to 2 bytes) via pad(entry.getSize(), border) (lines 254–258).
  - Marks entryEOF = true and, if “new-CRC”, compares the checksum (lines 259–264), then returns -1 to the caller.

3) Padding consumption is unreliable
- pad(long, int) uses a single call to InputStream.skip to discard the padding (lines 203–209). However, InputStream.skip is not guaranteed to skip the requested amount in one call; it may skip fewer bytes (including zero), and pad neither loops nor verifies it skipped all of the required padding.
- As a result, after finishing an entry, some padding bytes may remain unread. The next call to getNextEntry() tries to read the next header’s magic bytes but actually consumes leftover padding. This misaligns the stream and ultimately leads to an unexpected EOF when readFully (inside the header-reading logic) can’t get enough bytes for a valid header.

4) EOF propagation during data read is not handled
- In read(byte[], int, int), the code doesn’t handle tmpread == -1 from the underlying stream (line 273). If the underlying stream signals EOF prematurely (for any reason), the method returns -1 without:
  - marking entryEOF,
  - consuming required padding,
  - or reporting a truncated entry.
- Subsequent closeEntry() (called by getNextEntry()) will then read until -1 and stop without padding, so the next header read starts at the wrong position, again causing misalignment and an EOF/parse failure.

5) Impact across archives
- The above issues affect archives produced both by the library’s own writer and external tools (e.g., macOS cpio). Even valid archives can fail if skip doesn’t advance fully during padding, because the reader assumes padding is fully consumed after a single skip call.
- The test’s unarchive loop depends on read’s end-of-entry behavior to leave the stream positioned exactly at the next header. Because padding is not reliably consumed, the next header read fails with “unexpected EOF”.

Summary of root causes
- pad(long, int) is incorrect: it must ensure that all padding bytes are consumed, looping until the exact number of bytes is skipped/read or throwing an EOFException if not possible.
- read(byte[], int, int) does not handle underlying -1 correctly for in.read(...), which can mask truncated input and leave the stream in a corrupted state for the next entry.

These defects explain why unarchiving can fail with unexpected EOF for both internally generated and external (OS X) CPIO archives.

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
